scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. AITA?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). This is a **common family dynamic**, but it’s **painful when it feels like a rejection**. - **Loss of Control**: Ideas are **powerful**. Taking one without permission is like **someone writing your life story and publishing it without you**. It’s a **violation of autonomy**. His tears aren’t about money—they’re about **feeling like his mind was stolen**. --- ### **3. Many people **execute poorly** but still deserve credit for their contributions. - **Ideas Are Collaborative**: The best businesses (e.g., Apple, Google) are built on **teamwork**. Your dad’s idea might have been incomplete, but it was **his intellectual property**. - **Passivity ≠ Failure**: Your dad might not have "gotten things done" because he was **distracted by other ideas, health, or life circumstances**. Assuming he’s "lazy" is unfair. --- ### **4. What Should Have Happened? (A Better Path)** 1. **Discuss It First**: Before acting, **ask your dad**: - *"Dad, I love this idea. Can we explore how to make it happen together?"* - If he’s hesitant, offer to **handle the execution** while he provides guidance. 2. **Propose a Partnership**: Even if he’s not "business-savvy," he could have **advisory rights** or a **small stake** (e.g., 30-50%). 3. **Give Him Credit**: If you proceed alone, **name the product after him** or **acknowledge him publicly** (e.g., "Inspired by my father’s vision"). 4. **Apologize for the Betrayal**: You can’t undo the past, but you can **acknowledge the harm**: - *"I should have asked you first. I took something that wasn’t mine to take, and I’m sorry for that."* 5. **Rebuild Trust**: Offer to **share profits long-term** or **involve him in future decisions** to show you respect his role. --- ### **5.
